title: Suing on the company's behalf
subtitle: The statutory derivative claim and the two-stage permission test
objectives: State the statutory basis of a derivative claim under Part 11 of the Companies Act 2006 and explain how it replaced the common-law exception to Foss v Harbottle
Describe the two-stage permission procedure, including the mandatory refusal grounds and the discretionary factors the court must consider
Apply the permission test to a fact pattern and predict, with reasons, whether a court is likely to grant permission to continue a derivative claim

leadingAuthorities.role: The statutory scheme for derivative claims: what they are, and the two-stage permission procedure that controls them
The proper claimant and majority rule principles the statutory scheme was built to replace, not abolish outright

leadingAuthorities.citation: Iesini v Westrip Holdings Ltd [2009] EWHC 2526 (Ch)
leadingAuthorities.role: Leading guidance on the discretionary factors and the 'hypothetical director' test, and on why courts have proved restrictive

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Lesson 9 established that shareholders can sometimes ratify a director's breach. This lesson asks the opposite question: what happens when the wrongdoing directors control the company and simply refuse to sue themselves? A single shareholder cannot usually step in and sue on the company's own claim — that would contradict the very idea of separate personality from Lesson 1. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You can name the two stages — this lesson checks whether you can predict how a court will actually use its discretion.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans towards fact patterns that require you to work through the permission factors and reach a reasoned prediction, not just recite them.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and fix the Foss v Harbottle background first — the whole statutory scheme in ss 260-264 only makes sense as a controlled exception to that rule, not a free-standing shareholder right to sue.

overview.hook: A company is wronged by its own directors. The company itself, controlled by those same directors, does nothing about it — obviously it won't sue itself. A single minority shareholder, furious and armed with clear evidence, wants to bring the claim instead. Can they? The answer used to turn on a maze of nineteenth-century exceptions nobody could apply with confidence. Since 2006 it turns on a statutory gateway with two locked doors, and courts have made a point of keeping both of them mostly shut.

parts.heading: Foss v Harbottle: why an individual shareholder usually can't sue for a wrong to the company
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the story before naming the doctrine
body: Two minority shareholders in a company sued its directors, alleging the directors had defrauded the company by selling it land they owned personally at an inflated price. The claim looked strong on the facts. The court dismissed it anyway, for a reason that had nothing to do with the merits: the wrong, if it existed, was a wrong done to the company, not to the shareholders personally, so the company — not any individual member — was the proper claimant to sue for it.

Foss v Harbottle is usually distilled into two linked ideas. The proper claimant rule says a wrong done to the company can only be remedied by an action brought by the company itself, because the company is the entity whose property or rights were affected — precisely the separate-personality logic from Lesson 1. The majority rule principle adds that where the alleged wrong is something the company could, by ordinary resolution, decide to ratify or not pursue, the courts will not let a minority override that internal decision by suing regardless.

Taken together, these rules make obvious sense when the company's decision-making genuinely reflects an independent view. They become a serious problem when the wrongdoers are themselves in control of that decision-making — when the people who would have to authorise the lawsuit are the very people being sued. Nineteenth- and twentieth-century case law developed a patchwork of common-law exceptions to cover that situation (fraud on the minority chief among them), but the exceptions were notoriously uncertain in scope. Part 11 of the Companies Act 2006 replaced that patchwork with a single statutory gateway.

components.definition: The principle from Foss v Harbottle that a wrong done to a company can only be sued on by the company itself, not by an individual shareholder claiming to act on its behalf — the starting obstacle every derivative claim must overcome.

interaction.prompt: Under the proper claimant rule in Foss v Harbottle, who is generally entitled to sue for a wrong done to the company itself?
options: The company
Any individual shareholder who objects to the conduct
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The company is the proper claimant for a wrong done to it — an individual shareholder needs a specific gateway, like the statutory derivative claim, to sue on the company's behalf.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The proper claimant for a wrong done to the company is the company itself, not an individual shareholder acting alone. That's exactly the obstacle the statutory derivative claim exists to get past, in controlled circumstances.

parts.heading: Section 260: what a derivative claim actually is
parts.voice: statute-first — works from the text outward
body: Section 260 defines the modern derivative claim narrowly and precisely. It is a claim by a member of the company, but brought in respect of a cause of action vested in the company, not the member — the member is only the person bringing the proceedings; any remedy obtained belongs to the company. The cause of action must arise from an actual or proposed act or omission involving negligence, default, breach of duty or breach of trust by a director (or former director, or a shadow director).

Section 260(3) makes clear the claim can be brought against the director in question or against another person implicated in the same conduct — useful where a director has diverted a profit to a third party who knowingly received it. Critically, s 260(2) confirms that a derivative claim may now only be brought under this Chapter, or under an order of the court in unfair prejudice proceedings under s 994 (the subject of Lesson 11) — the old common-law derivative action is gone. This is the point students most often get backwards: the 2006 Act did not simply add a new option alongside the old common-law exceptions; it replaced them entirely with a single, more tightly controlled route.

Notice, too, what s 260 does not require: the director's conduct need not be dishonest, and the member bringing the claim need not show they were personally wronged. It is enough that the company has a cause of action against a director for negligence, default, breach of duty or breach of trust, and that a member wants to pursue it because the company itself will not.

components.text: (1) This Chapter applies to proceedings in England and Wales or Northern Ireland by a member of a company (a) in respect of a cause of action vested in the company, and (b) seeking relief on behalf of the company. This is referred to as a 'derivative claim'. (2) A derivative claim may only be brought (a) under this Chapter, or (b) in pursuance of an order of the court in proceedings under section 994. (3) A derivative claim under this Chapter may be brought only in respect of a cause of action arising from an actual or proposed act or omission involving negligence, default, breach of duty or breach of trust by a director of the company. The cause of action may be against the director or another person (or both).
elements: Brought by a member, but in respect of a cause of action vested in the company
Any relief obtained belongs to the company, not the claimant member
Available only under this Chapter or via a s 994 unfair prejudice order — the old common-law derivative action is abolished
Must arise from a director's (or former/shadow director's) negligence, default, breach of duty or breach of trust
May be brought against the director, another implicated person, or both

interaction.prompt: Under s 260(2), what happened to the common-law derivative action that existed before the Companies Act 2006?
options: It was replaced — a derivative claim may now only be brought under Part 11 of the Act, or via a court order in s 994 unfair prejudice proceedings
It was left untouched and now runs in parallel with the statutory scheme
It was preserved but only for public companies
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Section 260(2) is exhaustive: the statutory derivative claim, or a s 994 court order, are now the only routes. There is no surviving free-standing common-law derivative action.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at s 260(2)'s wording — 'may only be brought' under the Chapter or via a s 994 order. That closes off the old common-law route entirely rather than running it alongside the new statute.

parts.heading: Stage 1: the paper filter, and the mandatory refusal grounds
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Sections 261-263 build a two-stage procedure designed to weed out weak or improper claims before the company or its directors are even put to the expense of responding. At stage 1, the member applies for permission to continue the claim, and the application is considered by the court on the member's evidence alone, without the defendant being notified. Section 261(2) requires the court to dismiss the application at this stage, of its own motion, if the evidence filed by the member does not disclose a prima facie case for permission to be given — in other words, if the claim is hopeless on its face, it goes no further. If the claim survives this filter, the court may give directions for evidence from the company and adjourn the application to a full stage 2 hearing.

Section 263 then supplies two mandatory refusal grounds that apply if the claim reaches the discretionary stage: under s 263(2), the court must refuse permission if it is satisfied that a person acting in accordance with s 172 (the duty to promote the success of the company, from Lesson 6) would not seek to continue the claim, or that the act or omission has been authorised or ratified by the company (subject to the Cook v Deeks-style limits on ratification from Lesson 9). These are not factors to weigh — if either is made out, permission must be refused, full stop.

The two-stage structure exists precisely to stop derivative claims being used as a cheap way to harass a company's management: a claim has to clear an initial paper hurdle, then clear two absolute bars, before the court even turns to weighing the discretionary factors that follow.

components.title: The permission procedure, step by step
components.description: How a derivative claim moves from application to a decision on permission.

nodes.label: Member applies for permission to continue (s 261(1)), on notice to no one
Stage 1: court reviews the member's evidence alone
No prima facie case disclosed → court must dismiss (s 261(2))
Prima facie case shown → court may direct evidence from the company and adjourn to a full hearing
Stage 2: mandatory refusal grounds under s 263(2) — hypothetical director wouldn't continue, or conduct authorised/ratified
If neither mandatory ground applies, court weighs the discretionary s 263(3) factors

components.textAlternative: A member applies for permission without notifying anyone else. At stage 1 the court reviews only the member's evidence; if it discloses no prima facie case, the application is dismissed. If it does, the court can order evidence from the company and adjourn to a full hearing. At that hearing, the court must refuse permission if either mandatory ground under s 263(2) applies. Only if neither applies does the court go on to weigh the discretionary factors in s 263(3).

interaction.prompt: Put these stages of the permission procedure in the order they occur.
items: The member applies for permission to continue a derivative claim
The court reviews the member's evidence alone for a prima facie case
If a prima facie case is shown, the court may seek evidence from the company
The court checks whether either mandatory refusal ground under s 263(2) applies
If neither mandatory ground applies, the court weighs the discretionary s 263(3) factors
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the pipeline: a paper filter first, then two absolute bars, and only then genuine judicial discretion. Most claims that fail, fail at one of the first three steps.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — the prima facie filter comes before the company is even asked to respond, and the mandatory refusal grounds must be checked before the court ever reaches the discretionary balancing exercise.

parts.heading: Iesini v Westrip Holdings: the hypothetical director and why courts are so cautious
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the hard question before resolving it
body: Here's the question s 263(3) leaves genuinely open: even where a claim clears the mandatory bars, how should a court actually decide whether to let it proceed? Section 263(3) lists factors the court must take into account, including whether the member is acting in good faith, the importance a person acting under s 172 would attach to continuing the claim, whether the conduct could be, or has been, ratified, whether the company has decided not to pursue the claim, and the views of members with no personal interest in the matter.

Iesini v Westrip Holdings is the leading guidance on how to apply these factors in practice. Lewison J worked through the s 263(3) list systematically, and gave particular weight to what has become known as the 'hypothetical director' test: would a director acting in accordance with s 172 — promoting the company's success for the benefit of its members as a whole — regard continuing this particular claim as being in the company's interests, taking into account the cost, the prospects of success, the likelihood of recovering anything from the defendant, and the disruption litigation would cause?

Applying that test on the facts before him, Lewison J refused permission. The claim had weak prospects, and — crucially — even a director acting entirely properly could reasonably conclude the litigation wasn't worth pursuing given the costs and the doubtful recoverability of any judgment. Iesini has since become the standard citation for the proposition that derivative claims face a genuinely high bar in practice: the statutory scheme was drafted to widen access to the courts compared to the old common law, but the courts applying it have proved consistently restrictive, refusing permission far more often than granting it.

components.factsShort: Minority shareholders sought permission to bring a derivative claim against former directors, alleging mismanagement had caused the company to lose a valuable mining licence.
components.ratioShort: Permission should be refused where a hypothetical director acting under s 172 would not regard continuing the claim as in the company's interests, taking into account cost, prospects of success and likely recovery.

expanded.facts: Westrip Holdings had held an interest in a valuable Mongolian mining licence, which was lost following what the claimant shareholders alleged was serious mismanagement by the company's former directors. Minority shareholders sought the court's permission under s 261 to bring a derivative claim against those directors on the company's behalf, since the company (now under different control) had not itself pursued the claim.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Lewison J worked through the s 263(3) factors in detail, holding that the central question at the discretionary stage is whether a director acting in accordance with the s 172 duty would think it in the company's interests to continue the claim — weighing realistically the costs of litigation, the strength of the case on the merits, and the practical likelihood of recovering anything worthwhile from the defendants, rather than treating the existence of an arguable cause of action as sufficient on its own.
expanded.significance: Iesini remains the standard reference point for how English courts apply the discretionary stage of the permission test. It confirms that a technically arguable claim is not enough: the court asks a commercially realistic question about whether pursuing the litigation actually serves the company's interests, which is precisely why permission is refused in the clear majority of reported applications.

interaction.prompt: In this passage adapted from Iesini v Westrip Holdings, highlight the sentence stating the hypothetical director test.
interaction.passage: Counsel for the shareholders submitted that, since the underlying allegations of mismanagement were arguable, permission should follow more or less automatically. The court disagreed. The central question at this stage of the inquiry is whether a director acting in accordance with the section 172 duty to promote the success of the company would think it in the company's interests to continue the claim, having regard realistically to its cost, its prospects of success, and the likelihood of actually recovering anything of value from the proposed defendants.
interaction.ratioSentence: The central question at this stage of the inquiry is whether a director acting in accordance with the section 172 duty to promote the success of the company would think it in the company's interests to continue the claim, having regard realistically to its cost, its prospects of success, and the likelihood of actually recovering anything of value from the proposed defendants.

parts.heading: Why the statutory route is a narrow gate, not an open door
parts.voice: reflective — closes the lesson by weighing the doctrine against its purpose
body: It's worth being honest about the gap between what Part 11 promised and what it has delivered. The Law Commission and Parliament designed the statutory derivative claim to be more accessible than the old common-law exceptions, which had become a byword for procedural uncertainty. In practice, reported case law since 2006 shows courts refusing permission considerably more often than granting it — Iesini is one of many examples, not an outlier.

This matters for how you answer a problem question. The trap is treating 'the director clearly breached a duty' as the end of the analysis. It's the beginning: even a strong claim on the merits can fail at the discretionary stage if a hypothetical director, thinking commercially, would not regard the litigation as worth the company's money and management time. Conversely, weak evidence of the underlying breach will usually fail even earlier, at the stage 1 prima facie filter, before the discretionary factors are ever reached.

The examiner's fact pattern will typically hand you a clear breach and then bury the real issue in the surrounding facts: is the company genuinely refusing to sue because the wrongdoers control it, or because an independent board has made a considered commercial decision not to pursue a claim with poor prospects? Only the first scenario is what Part 11 was built for.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often conclude that once a clear breach of director's duty is established, permission for a derivative claim should follow as a matter of course.
components.whyItsWrong: Establishing a breach only gets a claimant past the starting line. The mandatory refusal grounds and the discretionary s 263(3) factors — especially the hypothetical director test from Iesini — mean the court asks a separate, commercially realistic question about whether continuing the litigation actually serves the company's interests. A strong claim on the merits can still fail permission on cost, prospects of recovery, or the disruption of litigation.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact most likely to lead a court to refuse permission under the Iesini hypothetical director test, even though the underlying breach looks arguable.
interaction.scenarioText: A minority shareholder seeks permission to sue a former director for breach of duty. The alleged loss is modest, the former director has no assets and lives abroad, and litigation costs are estimated to exceed any plausible recovery several times over.
tappableSpans: seeks permission to sue a former director
the former director has no assets and lives abroad
litigation costs are estimated to exceed any plausible recovery
interaction.correctSpan: litigation costs are estimated to exceed any plausible recovery
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. A hypothetical director weighing the company's interests would focus on whether the litigation is worth pursuing in practical, commercial terms — and spending more on costs than could ever be recovered is exactly the kind of fact that tips the balance towards refusing permission, regardless of how arguable the underlying breach is.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The breach being arguable isn't the deciding fact here — Iesini asks whether a hypothetical director would think the litigation worth pursuing. Look for the fact that speaks to cost versus realistic recovery, which is the clearest signal a court will weigh against continuing the claim.

testPool.prompt: Name the two mandatory grounds on which a court must refuse permission to continue a derivative claim under s 263(2).
acceptableAnswers: hypothetical director wouldn't continue the claim, and the conduct was authorised or ratified
testPool.modelAnswer: The court must refuse permission if a person acting under s 172 would not seek to continue the claim, or if the act or omission has been authorised or ratified by the company.

testPool.prompt: At the stage 1 permission filter under s 261, does the court hear evidence from the defendant director?
options: No — stage 1 is decided on the member's evidence alone
Yes — both sides must be heard at every stage

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a route by which a derivative claim can now be brought, under s 260(2)?
options: Under Part 11 of the Companies Act 2006
Under an order of the court in s 994 unfair prejudice proceedings
Under the surviving common-law derivative action alongside the statutory scheme
testPool.trapExplanation: Section 260(2) is exhaustive. There is no surviving common-law derivative action running alongside the statute — Part 11 replaced it entirely, leaving only the statutory route and the s 994 order route.

testPool.prompt: Order the reasoning steps a court follows once a derivative claim application reaches a full stage 2 hearing.
items: Check whether a hypothetical director under s 172 would not continue the claim
Check whether the conduct has been authorised or ratified by the company
If either mandatory ground applies, refuse permission
If neither applies, weigh the discretionary s 263(3) factors, including good faith and the views of independent members

testPool.prompt: Under s 260(3), a derivative claim's cause of action must arise from a director's conduct involving which of the following?
options: Negligence, default, breach of duty or breach of trust
Any conduct the member personally finds objectionable
Only conduct that is also a criminal offence

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that establishing a clear breach of a director's duty is, by itself, enough to obtain permission to continue a derivative claim?
sliderLabels: Confident — a clear breach is enough
Not confident — more than a clear breach is required
testPool.correctPosition: Not confident — more than a clear breach is required
testPool.explanation: Not confident is correct. Even a clear breach must still survive the s 261 prima facie filter, the s 263(2) mandatory refusal grounds, and the s 263(3) discretionary factors — including whether a hypothetical director would regard the litigation as worth pursuing.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that would most strongly help a member show the company's refusal to sue reflects wrongdoer control, rather than an independent commercial decision.
testPool.scenarioText: A company's board consists of three directors, two of whom are alleged to have diverted a lucrative contract to themselves. Those same two directors voted at a board meeting to decide the company would take no legal action against themselves, over the objection of the third, independent director.
tappableSpans: diverted a lucrative contract to themselves
voted at a board meeting to decide the company would take no legal action against themselves
over the objection of the third, independent director
testPool.correctSpan: voted at a board meeting to decide the company would take no legal action against themselves
testPool.explanation: The alleged wrongdoers using their own board votes to decide the company will not sue them is the clearest sign the 'company's decision' is not an independent one at all — exactly the scenario the statutory derivative claim exists to address.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario is more likely to satisfy the Iesini hypothetical director test in favour of granting permission?
testPool.scenarioA: The alleged breach caused a substantial, well-evidenced loss; the defendant director has significant assets from which any judgment could realistically be recovered; and estimated litigation costs are modest relative to the likely recovery.
testPool.scenarioB: The alleged breach is weakly evidenced, the defendant has no recoverable assets, and litigation costs are projected to exceed any plausible recovery several times over.
testPool.explanation: A is the stronger candidate for permission: a hypothetical director weighing cost, prospects of success and likely recovery would see a claim worth pursuing. B fails on nearly every factor Iesini identifies as relevant — weak evidence, no recoverable assets, and costs dwarfing any plausible recovery.

testPool.prompt: A minority shareholder applies for permission to continue a derivative claim. At the stage 1 review, the evidence filed shows only a vague, unsubstantiated allegation with no supporting documentation of any breach. What is the likely outcome?
options: The court must dismiss the application at stage 1, since the evidence discloses no prima facie case under s 261(2)
The court must still hold a full stage 2 hearing with evidence from the company
The court will grant permission automatically, since any member is entitled to bring a derivative claim
testPool.explanation: Section 261(2) requires the court to dismiss the application at stage 1, without input from the company or the defendant, if the member's own evidence does not disclose a prima facie case — a vague, unsubstantiated allegation is exactly the kind of application this filter exists to catch early.

testPool.prompt: A derivative claim seeks damages from a former director for breach of duty. If the claim succeeds, who receives the damages?
options: The company
The member who brought the claim, personally

testPool.prompt: Freya, a 5% shareholder in Harrow Components Ltd, discovers that the company's two other directors (who together hold 90% of the shares) diverted a profitable supply contract to a company they jointly own, breaching s 175. The board has taken no action against themselves. Freya wants to bring a derivative claim. Analyse whether she is likely to obtain permission to continue it.
factsToOrder: The two directors, holding 90% of the shares, diverted a corporate opportunity to themselves
The board (controlled by the wrongdoing directors) has taken no action
Freya holds only 5% of the shares
The alleged breach appears well-evidenced and the diverted contract was lucrative

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Freya, a minority shareholder, is likely to obtain permission under ss 260-264 to continue a derivative claim against the two controlling directors.
modelAnswer.rule: A derivative claim under s 260 may be brought in respect of a cause of action arising from a director's breach of duty. The court must first find a prima facie case (s 261(2)), then check the mandatory refusal grounds under s 263(2) — including whether a hypothetical director under s 172 would continue the claim — before weighing the discretionary s 263(3) factors, applying the Iesini approach.
modelAnswer.application: The alleged breach (diverting a corporate opportunity, engaging s 175) appears well-evidenced, which should satisfy the stage 1 prima facie filter. The board's inaction reflects wrongdoer control rather than an independent commercial decision, since the same directors who profited also control the decision not to sue — this weighs against the mandatory refusal ground being made out. Applying Iesini, a hypothetical director weighing cost, prospects of success and likely recovery would plausibly regard a well-evidenced, lucrative diversion as worth pursuing, particularly given the size of the profit diverted.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Freya has a reasonable prospect of obtaining permission: the claim appears to clear the prima facie filter, the mandatory refusal grounds are unlikely to bar it given wrongdoer control, and the discretionary factors point towards permission being granted, though the outcome ultimately turns on the court's assessment of cost and recoverability.

testPool.prompt: Which statement best captures the relationship between Foss v Harbottle and the statutory derivative claim?
options: Part 11 of the 2006 Act replaced the old common-law exceptions to Foss v Harbottle with a single statutory gateway, but the underlying proper claimant and majority rule principles still explain why a controlled, permission-based route is needed at all
Foss v Harbottle was overruled by the Companies Act 2006 and no longer has any relevance
The statutory derivative claim exists entirely independently of Foss v Harbottle and shares no conceptual link with it
testPool.trapExplanation: Foss v Harbottle was not overruled — it remains the reason a derivative claim needs a permission gateway at all. The 2006 Act replaced the uncertain common-law exceptions to it with a structured statutory procedure, rather than discarding the underlying principle.

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, adapted from s 263(3) commentary, highlight the sentence identifying the factor courts treat as carrying the most weight in practice.
testPool.passage: Section 263(3) lists several factors, including the good faith of the applicant and the views of independent members. In practice, however, courts applying Iesini have tended to give the greatest weight to whether a director acting under section 172 would regard continuing the claim as being in the company's interests, having regard to cost, prospects of success and likely recovery. Good faith and the views of disinterested members are usually treated as supporting, rather than displacing, that central commercial inquiry.
testPool.ratioSentence: In practice, however, courts applying Iesini have tended to give the greatest weight to whether a director acting under section 172 would regard continuing the claim as being in the company's interests, having regard to cost, prospects of success and likely recovery.

testPool.prompt: A shareholder seeks permission for a derivative claim over a director's honest but careless decision that caused a small loss. The company's independent, disinterested shareholders, fully informed, have already voted to ratify the conduct under s 239. What is the most likely outcome of the permission application?
options: Permission is likely to be refused, since valid ratification by an independent, informed majority is a mandatory ground for refusal under s 263(2)
Permission is irrelevant here, since ratification has no bearing on a derivative claim
Permission must be granted regardless, since any shareholder has an absolute right to bring a derivative claim
testPool.explanation: Section 263(2) makes valid authorisation or ratification a mandatory refusal ground. Because this is an honest, non-expropriating breach of the kind Lesson 9 confirmed can be ratified by an independent, informed majority, the ratification is effective and permission should be refused.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The single most common mistake in this lesson's test items is stopping the analysis once a breach of duty is established. A derivative claim then has to clear a prima facie filter, two mandatory bars, and a discretionary, commercially realistic test — Iesini's hypothetical director — before permission follows. A strong claim on the merits can still fail on cost and recoverability alone.
